title: Are bananas and Brazil nuts radioactive?
hook: Yes, a tiny bit. There’s even a "banana dose".
summary: Slightly: bananas contain potassium-40 and Brazil nuts can carry radium, in very small doses.

cardBlocks.text: Bananas contain natural radioactive material: potassium-40, one of the naturally occurring forms of potassium. It is so familiar that it became an informal unit, the "banana equivalent dose", used to explain tiny radiation doses. Eating an average banana works out to about 0.1 microsieverts, and the dose doesn’t build up, because the body gets rid of extra potassium in urine.

Brazil nuts can contain traces of radium, another radioactive element. The trees have a very extensive root system that can concentrate radium when it is present in the soil. It is a small dose, though higher than in most foods.
Bananas and Brazil nuts carry a little natural radioactivity, in very small doses.

deepDiveBlocks.text: A kilogram of Brazil nuts can have between 40 and 260 becquerels of radium activity. One popular-science magazine goes as far as saying radium levels can be a thousand times those of other foods.
The "banana dose" is not an official unit: it was created to explain very small radiation doses and risks to the public.
